sections.body:
The dating market is a metaphor for the meeting of people who are looking for a partner. It is a way of talking, not a place and not an institution. People reach for it when they want to describe the shape of a situation: how many people are looking, what they are looking for, how many possible partners each of them can actually meet, and who gets to say yes.

The metaphor borrows two words from ordinary trade. **Supply** is the group of people who are available to be chosen. **Demand** is the group of wishes they are looking to satisfy. Put the two together and the meeting of the two sides looks like a transaction, and the size and shape of the possibilities is what the metaphor calls the market.

It describes some real things well. It says that the number of people available to one person is not the same for everybody: it depends on the city, the working hours, the language, the habits and the ordinary company of the people around you. It says that both sides can refuse, and that a refusal is normal rather than a judgement. And it says that what people look for changes across a life, so that a person who looks for something different this year is not making a mistake.

What it quietly assumes is worth naming, because the assumption is where the harm comes from. It assumes that a person is an item with a price. It assumes that everything a partner can be fits on one scale. It assumes that the choosing side and the chosen side are different kinds of person. This article keeps the first part, which is a way of describing incentives, and refuses the rest: a pattern is explained here, and no person is ranked.
examples: The dating market is a way of describing the situation, not a place you can visit.
Supply and demand are two groups of people, not two groups of goods.
He described the dating market, and he did not describe anybody in it.
The number of people she can actually meet is not the number on the screen.
sections.heading: What the dating market is

terms.example: They talked about the dating market for an hour without saying anything about either of them.
terms.gloss: A metaphor for the meeting of people who are looking for a partner.

terms.example: The supply was small where she lived, and the same people kept appearing.
terms.gloss: The group of people who are available to be chosen, counted as a group and not as individuals.

terms.example: The demand was for somebody who wanted a quiet life, and that changed who she met.
terms.gloss: The group of wishes that the people looking are trying to satisfy.

sections.body:
Read the metaphor literally and it runs like this. Every participant has something to offer and something they want. Two people meet when what one offers is what the other wants. Where the two do not meet, no match happens, and the work of finding one is the work of the market. From this the metaphor draws predictions that people then treat as facts: attention is scarce, so people compete for it; the person who wants something scarce has to offer more of what is plentiful; and the visible result is **strategic behaviour** — a polished profile, a certain way of talking, a move to a city where more single people live.

Three things break. First, **commodification**: the metaphor turns a person into a thing with a price, and from that moment the other person is a means to an end. Second, what a person looks for is not fixed. It changes with experience, with the last relationship, with the work and with the stage of life, often without the person noticing that it has changed. Third, people change, so the number the metaphor hands out is a snapshot and not a constant.

A fourth break is the one the market reading keeps forgetting: every participant is also choosing. The person you are assessing is assessing you, at the same time and for their own reasons. A market in which everybody buys and nobody sells is not a market; it is a meeting of choosers. And the things that decide a long relationship — patience, reliability, the way two people handle a bad week — have no price in the metaphor at all, because the metaphor has no column for them.

The last break is the one that turns the metaphor into a ranking. The metaphor says that every person carries a **mate value**: a number that can be set beside the number of another person. That number is an artefact of the metaphor, not a measurement of a human being. Once it is accepted, every conversation about the market becomes a conversation about who is worth more, and the people in the conversation stop being people.
examples: Strategic behaviour is what the incentives produce; it is not the same as a good person.
Commodification starts the moment a person is treated as a price.
Both of us were choosing; that is what the market reading leaves out.
A mate value is a number the metaphor invented, not a thing a person has.
sections.heading: How the metaphor works, and where it breaks

terms.example: The whole conversation turned her into a commodity, and she left the table.
terms.gloss: The treatment of a person as a product that can be valued and exchanged.

terms.example: Strategic behaviour won him the interview; it did not make him better at the work.
terms.gloss: Acting in a planned way to produce a result, rather than acting in the way that comes naturally.

terms.example: He talked about his mate value instead of asking what she wanted.
terms.gloss: The number the market metaphor assigns to a person, as if it could be measured and compared.

sections.body:
The vocabulary comes from two places: trade and economics on one side, and the study of how people pair on the other. The words below are the ones that turn up in ordinary arguments about the market, and each of them says something precise.

Four of them describe the situation itself. **Market thickness** is how many potential partners a person can actually meet, given where they live and how their life is arranged; a thin market is one where the same few people keep appearing. **Bargaining power** is the capacity to say no without losing the chance of the thing you want; it is high when you have other plans and low when the alternative is nothing at all. **Choice overload** is the state in which the number of options makes the choosing harder instead of easier. **The price of choice** is the effort the chooser pays to make the choice, and it is paid in evenings, attention and doubt.

Two more words describe how two people are matched to each other. **Homogamy** is pairing with somebody similar in background, position or values. **Hypogamy** is pairing with somebody who has less of a valued resource — income, education, position — than the chooser. The third word of that family is **hypergamy**, and it is the subject of this article.
examples: The market was thin where she lived, and she met the same people again and again.
Her bargaining power came from having other plans that week.
Too many profiles, and the choosing turned into work instead of pleasure.
When one partner earns more, the pairing is hypogamy from one side and hypergamy from the other.
sections.heading: The words the subject uses

terms.example: A thin market was the real problem: she kept meeting the same people.
terms.gloss: How many potential partners a person can actually meet, given where they live and how their life is arranged.

terms.example: Her bargaining power came from having other plans that week.
terms.gloss: The capacity to say no without losing the chance of the thing you want.

terms.example: Too many profiles, and the choosing turned into work rather than pleasure.
terms.gloss: The state in which too many options make the choosing harder instead of easier.

terms.example: The price of choice was an evening spent reading instead of meeting anybody.
terms.gloss: The effort a person pays to choose among the options available.

terms.example: Homogamy is the word for the couple who grew up in the same kind of city.
terms.gloss: Pairing with a person who is similar in background, position or values.

terms.example: When one partner earns more, the pairing is hypogamy from one side and hypergamy from the other.
terms.gloss: Pairing with a person who has less of a valued resource, such as income, education or position, than the chooser.

sections.body:
Hypergamy is the hypothesis that people tend to pair with somebody who has more of a valued resource than they have themselves: more income, more education, a higher position, a steadier job. It is often described as marrying up, and the phrase hides the fact that the direction can be read from either side of a pair. A match in which one partner moves up in the counted resource is a match in which the other partner moves down.

The hypothesis makes predictions, and it explains some real things. It says the pattern is not random: across many pairings the direction is systematic rather than accidental. It says the pattern should be visible in behaviour as well as in results — in who writes first, in who changes the plan, in who moves. And it says the direction can be counted, because the hypothesis names the resources that can be counted. It gives a reason why people invest in credentials and in earning, when the direction of pairing runs upward. It explains why two people with similar personal qualities can end up in very different pairs, and why the same person is the one who moves in one pairing and the one who stays in another. It gives a name to a pattern that people notice and cannot otherwise describe.

What it cannot explain is the shape of the exception. Many pairings do not follow the direction, and in some settings the pattern runs the other way. The hypothesis says nothing about the resources that have no column — patience, humour, care, the ability to be a team — and nothing about the fact that both sides choose and both sides gain. And when the counted resource changes, the direction of the pattern can change with it, which makes the single word *up* a poor description of a complicated arrangement.

The debate is open, and this article does not close it. Some accounts treat the direction as a structural result of the way work, money and standing are divided. Others treat it as an individual matter: what a person looks for, how it changes, and why one person settles for less in one resource and more in another. A third group of accounts points out that the direction flips with the resource, so that any claim about marrying up is really a claim about one particular resource in one particular place and time. These are different answers, not one answer with a spelling mistake in it. What all of them agree on is that the pattern exists to be explained; what they disagree about is what explains it.
examples: Hypergamy names a direction of pairing, and the direction can be read from either side.
The hypothesis explains the direction; it does not explain the pairs that go the other way.
Nothing is counted in that column, so the hypothesis has nothing to say about it.
The debate about hypergamy is still open, and it is open about the mechanism.
sections.heading: Hypergamy in practice: what it predicts and what it cannot explain

terms.example: Hypergamy names the direction of the pairing, and the direction can be read from either side.
terms.gloss: Pairing with a person who has more of a valued resource, such as income, education or position, than the chooser.

sections.body:
The same pattern gets more than one explanation, and the table sets them side by side. The first column names the account. The second says what the account predicts if it is right. The third says what it still cannot account for. The fourth says where the argument stands.

Read the fourth column carefully. In most of these rows the answer is the same: the argument is open. That is not a way of avoiding the question. It is the honest state of the subject, and an article that pretended otherwise would be teaching the reader a conclusion that the evidence does not carry.
examples: Two accounts can describe the same pattern and disagree about what produces it.
The fourth column is where the open questions sit.
I am not choosing between the accounts; I am checking what each one leaves out.
sections.heading: The hypothesis and the answers beside it

rows: The hypergamy hypothesis: a systematic direction of pairing.
Across many pairs, one partner carries more of a counted resource than the other, and the difference shows in behaviour as well as in results.
The pairs that do not follow the direction, and the pairs where the direction changes when the counted resource changes.
Open: how general the pattern is, in which resources and in which settings.
The homogamy pattern: people pair with others like themselves.
The two people in a pair are similar in background, position or values, and the pairing keeps that similarity.
The pairs where the two people are clearly unlike each other in exactly those ways.
Open: how much of the similarity is chosen, and how much is simply who is around to be met.
The two-sides account: both partners are choosing.
Each pair moves towards a point where each side gains what it values, and the gains are not counted in the same currency.
The pairs where one side gains much more than the other, and the pairs where neither side gains.
Open: how often two people actually value the same things.
The individual account: what a person looks for moves.
What one person looks for changes with experience, with the last relationship and with the stage of life, so the same person is not the same chooser twice.
The fact that similar patterns appear across many people at the same time and in the same direction.
Open: how much of the pattern is a shared constraint rather than a shared wish.
The local account: an ordinary reason behind one meeting.
One meeting happened for ordinary local reasons — the same class, the same office, the same friend — and no general law was at work.
Why those local reasons keep clustering in the same places, and in the same direction.
Not disputed as a description of one meeting; disputed as an explanation that goes beyond the local case.

sections.body:
The metaphor is useful exactly when it names an incentive and harmful exactly when it names a price. Six steps keep it on the right side of that line, and they take a few minutes.

The first three are about the words. Name the incentive instead of the person. Check the incentive against the person in front of you, because the model describes a general pattern and the person has a history and reasons of their own. And never let a model turn into a verdict: a model says what tends to happen, and it does not decide who deserves your time.

The last three are about the choice itself. Name what the metaphor leaves out, because those things are often the ones you actually want. Keep in mind that you are the chooser as well, and that being choosy is ordinary and needs no apology. And keep the vocabulary away from other people: not a weapon, not a compliment, not a way of talking about somebody you have only seen a profile of.
examples: The model explains the incentive; the decision is still mine.
He is answering the incentive, not answering me.
A pattern is not a verdict on the person in front of me.
I can say no without giving a reason, and I do not owe one.
sections.heading: How to use the metaphor without hurting yourself
steps: Name the incentive, not the person. If the model explains why somebody is trying harder, changing their plans or presenting themselves in a certain way, say that — and do not say that the person is worth more or worth less.
Check the incentive against the person in front of you. The model describes a general pattern; the person has a context, a history and reasons of their own.
Do not treat a model as a verdict. It says what tends to happen, not who is right for you and not what anybody is worth.
Name what the metaphor leaves out — the things you actually want, such as patience, reliability, humour and shared ordinary work — and put them on the same list.
Keep your side of the table in view. You are choosing too, and the right to say no needs no permission from a model.
Keep the vocabulary out of other people's mouths. Do not use the market language on a partner, on a colleague, or on somebody you have only seen a profile of.

sections.body:
The dating market is a contested metaphor, and it is often used in a way this article refuses: to sort people into a scale and to say who is at the top. Nothing here does that. There is no number for a person, and the idea of one is an artefact of the metaphor rather than a measurement of anybody.

A pattern is also not a verdict. Saying that many pairings move in one direction says nothing about the worth of either person in a particular pair, and nothing about a person's life. The same holds for the hypothesis: it describes something and it explains something, and it does not decide who should meet whom, who should be asked twice, or who should settle.

And this article is not a method for winning. It gives you vocabulary and a check. What you want in a partner is yours to name, and naming it plainly is more useful than any model: *I want somebody kind, calm, and interested in the same ordinary life I am already living.*
examples: There is no market value for a person, and the metaphor's number is not a measurement.
Describing a pattern is not passing a verdict on somebody.
Naming what I want is more useful than any model of my chances.
sections.heading: The ranking this article refuses

sections.body:
The first group talks about the metaphor without reducing people to prices. The second answers somebody who uses it as an excuse. The third describes what you are looking for, which is the part only you can write.

None of them needs a hard voice. The point is to be understood the first time, and to keep the conversation on the mechanism instead of on the worth of the people in it.
examples: The dating market is a useful way to talk about how people meet; it is not a way to rank them.
There are fewer people to meet here than there are apps to meet them in, and that changes what a search looks like.
I use the market metaphor to talk about incentives, not about people.
The market is not an excuse for treating people as prices.
You can explain your choices by the market, but you cannot use it to excuse treating me badly.
A model describes a situation; it does not give anybody the right to behave badly in it.
I am looking for somebody who is calm, funny and willing to do the dishes on a Tuesday.
I want a partner, not a project I am trying to finish.
I care more about how somebody treats a waiter than about what they do for work.
I want somebody I can be ordinary with on a Wednesday.
I am not looking for a rescue; I am looking for company.
The job and the money matter, but they are not the whole list, and I know which part of the list matters most to me.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: The dating market is a metaphor, not a law, and hypergamy is a hypothesis that people still argue about. After reading this you can explain what the metaphor describes and what it assumes, name the words the subject uses, state what the hypothesis predicts and what it cannot explain, compare it with the other answers for the same pattern, and use the vocabulary without turning people into a ranking.
item.title: The Dating Market and the Hypergamy Hypothesis
